claims.claim: Le Guin states that the chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised ed.), chapter 1, excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead

claims.claim: Le Guin observes of the Hurston passage she selects that the vocabulary is simple and familiar and the rhythm carries the power.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised ed.), chapter 1, excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the vocabulary is simple and familiar
claims.page: Steering the Craft ch.1, commentary before example III

claims.claim: Le Guin analyses Molly Gloss's prose as having changing sentence rhythms that embody and express the characters' emotions.

claims.quote: the changing sentence rhythms embody and express the emotions

claims.claim: Le Guin reports that the 'show, don't tell' rule leaves workshop writers afraid to describe the world they have invented.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy' (Los Angeles Times, 5 Jan 2003), on ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: They're afraid to describe the world they've invented.

claims.claim: Le Guin prescribes the opening chapter of The Return of the Native, a landscape description in which nothing happens, as the cure for that fear.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'On Rules of Writing, or, Riffing on Rechy' (Los Angeles Times, 5 Jan 2003), on ursulakleguin.com
claims.quote: a description of a landscape, in which absolutely nothing happens
claims.page: parenthesis in the 'show don't tell' paragraph

claims.claim: Le Guin disputes the belief that the narrator's voice distances the story, calling it the most intimate voice of all.

claims.quote: it's the most intimate voice of all

claims.quote: which involves and includes past, present, and future

claims.quote: their flow is perfectly clear, and follows the breath

claims.claim: Le Guin writes that in The Lord of the Rings punctuation comes just where the reader-aloud needs to pause.

claims.quote: Tolkien must have heard what he wrote.

verdicts.trueWording: The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence
verdicts.note: Lit Hub ch.1 raw page: 'The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence—to keep the story going.' Quote exact; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: vocabulary simple and familiar; above all the rhythm is powerful
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'In this one and the next, the vocabulary is simple and familiar; it's above all the rhythm that is powerful and effective. To read Hurston's sentences aloud...' Quote exact. Note the comment covers BOTH the Hurston (III) and Gloss (IV) passages, not Hurston alone — the claim's restriction to Hurston is true but narrower than the source.

verdicts.trueWording: changing sentence rhythms embody and express the characters' emotions
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'Molly Gloss's prose is quiet and subtle; its power and beauty come from the perfect placement and timing of the words, the music of their sound, and the way the changing sentence rhythms embody and express the emotions of the characters.' Quote exact; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: workshop writers afraid to describe the world they've invented
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'Thanks to "show don't tell," I find writers in my workshops who think exposition is wicked. They're afraid to describe the world they've invented.' Quote exact (curly apostrophes on page); every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: landscape description where nothing happens until a man appears
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim on the raw page and the prescription limb holds ('I make them read the first chapter of The Return of the Native'; 'If that won't cure them nothing will'). But the source sentence continues past the quoted cut: '...in which absolutely nothing happens UNTIL IN THE LAST PARAGRAPH A MAN IS SEEN, from far away, walking along a road.' The claim's unqualified 'in which nothing happens' drops that, and the quote as recorded is a mid-sentence truncation that must not be reused without the continuation or an ellipsis.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the claim's 'in which nothing happens' — the page says nothing happens *until in the last paragraph a man is seen walking along a road*

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator's voice is the most intimate voice of all
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'They believe the narrator's voice (ponderously described as "omniscient") distances the story — whereas it's the most intimate voice of all, the one that tells you what is in the characters' hearts, and in yours.' Quote exact; the dispute limb is explicit in 'whereas'.

verdicts.trueWording: writers abandon narrative past for the inflexible present tense
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'The same fear of "distancing" leads writers to abandon the narrative past tense, which involves and includes past, present, and future, for the tight-focused, inflexible present tense. But distance lends enchantment...' Quote exact; the critical stance is carried by 'fear', 'far too much', 'restrict' and the closing 'But distance lends enchantment'.

verdicts.trueWording: narrative past tense involves and includes past, present, and future
verdicts.note: Raw page: '...the narrative past tense, which involves and includes past, present, and future...' Quote exact; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: even long sentences: flow perfectly clear, follows the breath
verdicts.note: Raw blog page quotes the essay: 'Even when the sentences are long, their flow is perfectly clear, and follows the breath; punctuation comes just where you need to pause; the cadences are graceful and inevitable.' Quote exact and attributed to Le Guin's Meditations on Middle-earth chapter, as the claim's source field states.

verdicts.trueWording: punctuation comes just where you need to pause
verdicts.note: Same quoted essay sentence on the raw blog page; the read-aloud frame is explicit ('it's a wonderful book to read aloud'). Quote exact; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Tolkien must have heard what he wrote
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'Le Guin observes that "Tolkien must have heard what he wrote."' Quote exact. The page's own verb is 'observes'; the claim's 'concludes from the read-aloud quality' is supplied by the surrounding context (the whole passage is about reading LotR aloud), not by an explicit inference marker on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Le Guin's language is plain, strong, and exact
verdicts.note: NEA PDF (12pp, extracted text), p.4 'Sources of Inspiration / The Language of Fantasy': 'Throughout A Wizard of Earthsea Le Guin's language is plain, strong, and exact; her tone grave and slightly formal; and the rhythm of her sentences carefully balanced and musical.' Authorship limb confirmed by the guide's Acknowledgments: 'Writer: Michael Dirda'.

verdicts.trueWording: her tone grave and slightly formal
verdicts.note: Same sentence on NEA PDF p.4; quote exact; Dirda named as the guide's writer in the Acknowledgments.

verdicts.trueWording: rhythm of her sentences carefully balanced and musical
verdicts.note: Same sentence on NEA PDF p.4; quote exact; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: occasional touches of alliteration and assonance recall Old English verse
verdicts.note: NEA PDF p.4: 'Note the occasional touches of alliteration and assonance—reminiscent of Old English verse—in such phrases as this: "Forest rises ridge behind ridge to the stone and snow of the heights."' Quote exact including the em dashes; every limb supported.
